unit.name: Exploration, epsilon-greedy choice, and DQN results
unit.description: Explains why greedy DQN can get stuck, introduces epsilon-greedy exploration, and recaps the final DQN training loop and empirical outcome.
unit.summary: A small three-action example shows that a randomly initialized Q-network can become stuck exploiting a modest reward and never visit the best action with reward 1000 [ts=4246s] [ts=4365s]. This motivates the exploration versus exploitation tradeoff: agents must sometimes try actions that do not currently look best to discover better rewards [ts=4384s] [ts=4446s]. Epsilon-greedy action choice adds randomness by taking a random action with probability epsilon and otherwise choosing the action with maximum predicted Q-value [ts=4571s] [ts=4602s]. The final DQN loop includes replay memory, terminal-state tracking, epsilon-greedy action selection, Bellman target estimation, and gradient-descent updates, after which the Breakout agent discovers the tunnel strategy behind the bricks [ts=4589s] [ts=4665s].

key_points.text: A greedy Q-network can get stuck if it never explores an action whose initial Q-value is lower but whose true reward is much higher.
The exploration-exploitation tradeoff is the need to balance trying new actions against using the currently best-known action.
Epsilon-greedy action selection takes a random action with probability epsilon and otherwise follows the greedy Q-network action.
The complete DQN loop combines Q-network initialization, replay memory, terminal-state tracking, epsilon-greedy choice, sampling from memory, and Bellman target training.
The trained Breakout agent discovers that tunneling the ball behind the bricks can finish the game more easily.
A practical way to evaluate RL improvement is to monitor rewards and, for competitive agents, compare models through self-play.
